II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00431

V. Muhammad al-Baqir (“He Who Opens” or “Splits Open,” meaning one who makes knowledge accessible). Born in Medina in 57/676; died there in 115/733. His grave is in al-Baqi. The many sayings attributed to him are especially rich in teachings about inner spiritual knowledge. In certain scenes borrowed from the infancy gospels and adapted in some Ismaili texts, he takes the place occupied by Jesus in the original stories.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00432

VI. Jafar al-Sadiq (“the Truthful,” “the Loyal”). Born in Medina in 80 or 82 AH/699 or 702 CE; died there in 148/765. His grave is in al-Baqi. He taught many pupils and disciples, and a very large number of traditions come from his teaching. Like that of his father, his work was decisive in the development of the different branches of Shiite thought.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00433

VII. Musa al-Kazim (“He Who Controls Himself”). Born in Medina in 128/745; died in Baghdad in 183/799. His tomb is at the shrine of Kazimayn, near Baghdad. Twelver Shiites recognize him as the Seventh Imam. His older brother, Imam Ismail, who died young, gave his name to the Ismaili Shiites, for whom the Imamate continued through Ismail's descendants. Here the Shiite family divides into the Twelver and Seven-Imam branches.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00434

VIII. Ali al-Rida (“He with Whom God Is Pleased”). Born in Medina in 153/770; died at Tus, in Khurasan, in 203/818. His tomb is at the famous shrine in Mashhad, one of the most important places of pilgrimage for Iranian Shiites. We have already seen how the Abbasid caliph al-Mamun, son of Harun al-Rashid, named him his intended successor. The Imam's early death—probably not an accident—ended that plan.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00435

But what could have come of it in any case? The Imam had accepted only under pressure. From the Shiite point of view, there could be no compromise with the direction in which the caliphs' politics had taken Islam. The Imams had to remain what they were: witnesses to a world beyond this world, a different order of reality.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00436
We can still hear the testimony of Imam Rida and of his father, Musa al-Kazim, in the substantial collection in which Shaykh Saduq Ibn Babuyeh (d. 381/991) preserved their main teachings and sermons.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00437

IX. Muhammad al-Jawad al-Taqi (“the Generous,” “the Devout”). Born in Medina in 195/811; died in Baghdad in 220/835. His grave is at the shrine of Kazimayn. With him begins the moving and tragic final group of Imams, all of whom died in the prime of life.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00438

X. Ali al-Hadi al-Naqi (“the Guide,” “the Pure One”) was born in Baghdad or Medina in 212 or 214 AH (827 or 830 CE). He died in Samarra in 254 AH (868 CE), in the military camp where the Abbasid caliph and his police had kept him a prisoner for twenty years. A number of teachings attributed to him carry profound meaning. His tomb is in the shrine at Samarra.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00439

XI. Hasan al-Zaki al-Askari (“the Upright One,” “the One Held in the Military Camp”) was born, perhaps in Medina, in 231 AH (845 CE), and died in Samarra in 260 AH (874 CE). He is a moving figure, and we will return to him at length towards the end of this book. Like his father, he is buried at the shrine in Samarra, an important place of Shiite pilgrimage.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00440

XII. Muhammad al-Qa'im, al-Mahdi is the most mysterious of these figures. He is called the One Who Rises (Qa'im), the Rightly Guided One (Mahdi), the Awaited One (Muntazar), the Proof or Guarantor of God (Hujjat), and the unseen master of the present age: the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Born in Samarra in 255 AH (869 CE), he disappeared on the very day his father died, 4 Shawwal 260 AH (24 July 874 CE). The entire final book of this work will explore this disappearance, known as the Occultation, what it means, and how it will end.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00441

Leaving aside their titles of honour, the Fourteen Immaculate Ones bear only seven personal names: Muhammad, Fatima, Ali, Hasan, Husayn, Ja'far, and Musa. The meaning of these Names beyond earthly life is one of the great themes of Shiite spiritual philosophy. The order in which the Fourteen briefly appear in our world is not seen as an accident of history. Their earthly succession reflects the order in which they first came into being, before time, in the fullness of the spiritual world—the order in which their beings of light answered the mysterious question, A-lastu bi-rabbikum? (“Am I not your Lord?”). That question resounded in a world before Adam and before anything visible had appeared on earth.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00442
Their brief lives in history therefore cannot show us the whole of who they are. Most of those lives were obscure to the people around them, and marked by grief, sorrow, and hardship.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00443

We must also see their other dimension: a spiritual depth hidden within the fragile, passing body. It still speaks to us through the teachings they gave their disciples, who asked them to explain the meaning of divine revelations. Each of these figures has a fuller identity, revealed from world to world and from one person's awareness to another, that goes infinitely beyond what could appear during a short earthly life. Each of the Twelve Imams deserves a book devoted to this fuller reality. The sources are abundant, and the task would be immense.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00444

Some diagrams show the timeless arrangement of their different ranks. We find them in the writings of scholars of divine wisdom, such as Haydar Amoli, who saw these patterns in their own visions. We also find them in popular Shiite religious art. One familiar Iranian devotional image places the Twelve Imams around the edge of a circle, with the Prophet Muhammad at its centre.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00445

Fatima, her face veiled and her head surrounded by the sun's radiance, connects the Prophet to the line of Imams. Sometimes she appears directly between the Prophet and the First Imam; sometimes she stands a little to the right. The Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam, is shown as a young boy. He marks one end of the line that also includes the Prophet, Fatima, and the First Imam.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00447

These images, which make the invisible figures present to the eye, arise from the deepest feelings of religious devotion. A religion reveals something of its most private secret in its sacred images and its prayers. That secret can never be fully expressed in human words. We would like to make the inner music of Shiite prayer perceptible here, but the subject would require a substantial book of its own.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00448

Because the Imam is “absent,” he cannot personally lead the community's formal prayers in the mosque. Believers can therefore also pray in their own private places of worship. Shiite Islam has developed an extensive body of prayers for personal devotion, known as du'a. This literature contains treasures of religious feeling and insight into the inner life of faith. It includes greetings addressed to each of the Twelve Imams according to the yearly, weekly, or daily calendar, as well as prayers that allow the believer to visit the Twelve—or, more precisely, all Fourteen Immaculate Ones—in the mind and spirit. Later, in Chapter V, we will return to one of these spiritual pilgrimages, the al-Ziyarat al-Jami'a. It begins:
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00449
Peace be upon you, members of the House of Prophecy, where the prophetic message has its dwelling, where the angels come one after another, where divine revelation descends…
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00450

But we cannot pass over another prayer, widely regarded as the Twelver Shiite prayer above all others. It is attributed to the great philosopher and theologian Nasir al-Din Tusi (d. 672 AH/1274 CE), who played such an important part in protecting the Shiite community when the Mongols captured Baghdad. The prayer is therefore known as the Davazdeh Imam-e Khwajeh-ye Nasir, or “The Twelve Imams of Khwajeh Nasir.” I see no decisive reason to reject this traditional attribution.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00451

In the introduction to the prayer, Tusi himself tells the story of its composition. He had wished to offer a scientific treatise he had written to al-Mu'tasim, who was to be the last Abbasid caliph of Baghdad (640–656 AH/1242–1258 CE).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00452

But the caliph found a tribute to the Twelve Imams at the beginning of the book, tore the manuscript apart, and threw it into the Tigris. Tusi decided that it would be wise to put some distance between himself and the caliph. He left for Samarkand, arriving while preparations were under way for the Mongol expedition that would bring the Abbasid caliphate to an end. During his journey, he dreamed that the Prophet and the First Imam appeared to him and urged him to compose a prayer praising the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00453
We will encounter a similar story in Book V, involving a prayer that Mir Damad heard in a visionary dream at the mosque in Qom.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00454

The full prayer, conceived as a spiritual pilgrimage, is too long to reproduce here. Our ellipses show how extensively we have shortened it. Among the passages omitted are the references to each of the Fourteen Ones' shrines—the burial places the worshipper visits in the imagination (as noted above). Our aim is simply to convey the rhythm of the prayer. Each passage has two movements: a changing invocation addressed to God, followed by a response voiced together by the worshippers.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00455

I. O God, honour and welcome the Prophet; sustain him and bless him… the Lamp that gives light, the shining Star… the Prince of Messengers, the Seal of the Prophets… Honour and peace be upon you, O Messenger of God, O Imam of Mercy, O intercessor for the community, O God's Witness before His creatures, O our prince and our lord… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00456

II. O God, honour and welcome the purest prince, the victorious Imam; sustain him and bless him… the manifestation of wonders and miracles… the blazing Meteor… the Centre of the Circle of Difficulties… the victorious Lion of God… the Imam of East and West… O brother of the Messenger of God, O husband of the Virgin… O God's Witness before His creatures, O our prince and our lord… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00457

III. O God, honour and welcome the glorious Lady; sustain her and bless her—the beautiful, the utterly pure, the wronged, the generous, the noble… who suffered so many sorrows in so short a life… Queen of Women, the Dark-Eyed One, Mother of the Imams… daughter of the greatest of prophets… the Immaculate Virgin, the deeply devout… Honour and peace be upon you and your descendants, O Fatima the Radiant, O daughter of Muhammad, God's Messenger… O God's Witness before His creatures, O our Lady and our sovereign… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00458

IV. O God, honour and welcome the chosen prince, the Imam of Hope; sustain him and bless him… who knew suffering, hardship, and pain, both in their visible and hidden forms… Honour and peace be upon you, O Hasan, O son of the Messenger of God, son of the Commander of the Faithful, son of Fatima the Radiant! O God's Witness before His creatures… O prince of the young people of Paradise… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00459

V. O God, honour and welcome the prince who renounced worldly pleasures, the Imam of Prayer; sustain him and bless him… adornment of pulpits and holy places, the One Tried by suffering and sorrow… Honour and peace be upon you, O Husayn ibn Ali! O martyr, O wronged one! Son of the Messenger of God, son of the Commander of the Faithful, son of Fatima the Radiant… O prince of the young people of Paradise… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00460

VI. O God, honour and welcome the father of the Imams and Lamp of the Community; sustain him and bless him… the One Who Knew Sorrow, the One Who Brought the Tradition to Life… Honour and peace be upon you, O Ali ibn Husayn, O al-Sajjad (foremost in worship), O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00461

VII. O God, honour and welcome the Moon of Moons, the Light of Lights, Guide of the Chosen and Prince of the Just; sustain him and bless him… a surging Ocean and a precious Pearl… Honour and peace be upon you, O Muhammad ibn Ali, O al-Baqir (the one who penetrates the depths of knowledge)… O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00462

VIII. O God, honour and welcome the faithful and utterly truthful prince; sustain him and bless him—the wise, the steadfast, the patient, the compassionate, the guide along the path, the one who gives his Shiite followers a generous draught of pure wine… Honour and peace be upon you, O Ja'far ibn Muhammad, O al-Sadiq… O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00463

IX. O God, honour and welcome the generous prince, the patient Imam, the one who knew how to master his anger; sustain him and bless him… the one surrounded by the brightest radiance of nobility… Honour and peace be upon you, O Musa ibn Ja'far, O al-Kazim, O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

X. O God, honour and welcome the purest prince, the wronged Imam, the martyr who died by poison; sustain him and bless him… the sage who knows the hidden knowledge, the full moon in a star-filled sky… companion of souls… Honour and peace be upon you, O Ali ibn Musa, O al-Rida, son of the Messenger of God… God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00465

XI. O God, honour and welcome the prince of justice, the noble-hearted, the generous; sustain him and bless him… the one who knows the secrets of the Beginning and the Return, guide to all people, refuge of his friends on the day when the caller raises his cry… the Imam in the tradition of Ahmad, the Light of Muhammad… Honour and peace be upon you, O Muhammad ibn Ali, O al-Taqi al-Jawad, O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00466

XII and XIII. O God, honour and welcome the two noble and perfect Imams; sustain them and bless them… twin suns, twin moons, twin lights… heirs to the two holy sanctuaries… both helpers of the human race… twin signs of right guidance… both of whom knew hardship and sorrow, both masters of generosity and goodness… Honour and peace be upon you both, O Ali ibn Muhammad and O Hasan ibn Ali! Upon you, O al-Naqi al-Hadi, and upon you, O al-Zaki al-Askari! Sons of the Messenger of God… God's Witnesses before His creatures… Both of you, intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00467

XIV. O God, honour and welcome the one who gathers into himself the Prophet's calling, the fierce courage of the Lion of God, the perfect purity of Fatima, the patience of Hasan, the bravery of Husayn, the devotion of al-Sajjad, the memorable teachings of al-Baqir, the traditions of Ja'far, the knowledge of al-Kazim, the arguments of al-Rida, the generosity and devotion of al-Jawad al-Taqi, the revered dignity of the two Askaris, the hiddenness of divine concealment, the One Who Rises (Qa'im) in truth… the Word of God… God's Witness, the One Who Triumphs by God's command… Imam in secret and Imam openly revealed, the one who drives away sorrow and grief… the generous, the noble-hearted, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, unseen lord of this age and representative of the All-Merciful, Imam of human beings and jinn… Honour and peace be upon you, O heir of Hasan Askari, O Imam of our time, O awaited One Who Rises, O guided one who guides others! Son of the Messenger of God… Witness of God before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00468

This is how Shiite hearts pray. At the end of the present work we will meet the last three Imams again, especially the moving figures of the Tenth and Eleventh, the two Askaris. Although the Abbasid government held them captive in the military camp at Samarra, they were preparing the way for the mysterious Twelfth Imam's brief appearance in this world. One of the surviving texts will then allow us to hear the distinctive tone of the prayers he inspires in those who make a spiritual pilgrimage to him.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00469

As we have already said, just as his ancestor Muhammad is the “Seal of the Prophets,” the Twelfth Imam is the Seal of the Muhammadan walayat: the final and fullest expression of the spiritual bond through which God's friends lead others into the mystery of divine manifestations. The Prophet and the Imam reveal the same original Light and the same Supreme Spirit (Ruh A'zam). The Prophet brings the outward message; the Imam discloses its inner meaning.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00470

Walayat is that inward reality—the spiritual truth contained within prophecy—while prophecy is its outward and visible form. Just as every prophet was a manifestation (mazhar) of the Seal of the Prophets, so every friend of God and every person initiated into the spiritual life manifests, in some measure, the one who is and will be the Muhammadan Seal of God's Friends. In the chapters that follow, we must explore this whole group of ideas more deeply.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
en-book-1-ch-2-s4
4. The Paradoxes Faced by Ismailism and Twelver Shiism
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00471

Even this brief account has allowed us to glimpse some of the defining features of Twelver Shiism: its central ideas, the direction of its spiritual life, and what we might call its focus on the Imam. What I can say here is necessarily only a beginning, a foundation for further work. And to give a rounded picture of Shiite thought and spirituality—without leaving out a vital part of Iranian Islam—we would now need to turn to its other main branch. This is the tradition sometimes described as the “Seveners,” but more commonly called Ismailism.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00472

As we have seen, Ismailism takes its name from its Seventh Imam, Ismail, the eldest son of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 148 AH/765 CE), who died before his father. The two great branches of Shiism part ways at the Seventh Imam. In Ismaili teachings about divine wisdom and the Imams, seven, rather than twelve, becomes the central number. I have outlined elsewhere the main differences between Ismailism and Twelver Shiism, so I will not repeat that discussion here. Both traditions still deserve a comprehensive study of their deepest ideas, and I hope to devote separate works to them. For now, I want simply to recall why the Ismaili religious tradition matters so much to the spiritual history of Iranian Islam.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00473

To begin with, any serious study of Shiism must return to its origins during the Prophet's own lifetime. It must therefore start before the movement divided into its two principal branches (alongside smaller branches, such as the Zaydis of Yemen). Such a study would need to bring together the traditional teachings of the Imams accepted by both principal branches. Together, these teachings make up an enormous body of material. Preserving and collecting them was above all the work of Twelver Shiites. Meanwhile, between the fourth/tenth and fifth/eleventh centuries, Ismaili thinkers produced their great syntheses of divine wisdom. These belonged to the Fatimid period, and some of the most important authors were Iranian: Abu Ya'qub Sijistani, al-Mu'ayyad Shirazi, Hamid al-Din Kirmani, Nasir-e Khusraw, and others.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00474

During the same period, Twelver Shiites—often living under extremely difficult conditions—were chiefly occupied with gathering the traditions of their Imams. They arranged these teachings systematically around the major subjects that would become standard in Shiite religious thought. Their patient care made possible a later achievement. When conditions improved for Twelver Shiism, the great Iranian theologian of the Safavid period, Muhammad Baqir Majlisi (d. 1110 AH/1698–99 CE), was able to work with a whole team of assistants to assemble this vast collection. In its older, stone-printed edition, it filled no fewer than twenty-six parts in fourteen large folio volumes. At the time of writing, a new printed edition was being prepared in Tehran.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00475

For various reasons, some traditions (hadith) were not included. Even so, the collection brings together the teachings of the Prophet and the Twelve Imams: the full body of sacred tradition (sunna) recognised by Twelver Shiism. It is not merely the basis for interpreting the deeper meaning of revelation. It is also an encyclopedia of spiritual knowledge. Its subjects include God's oneness (tawhid), prophecy, the Imams, the universe, human nature, and what happens at the end of time. It also explains religious rites and the practice of the sacred law (sharia).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00476
In short, it addresses both the inner meaning (batin) and the outward form (zahir) of religion.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00477

We have already seen how central this distinction is to Shiism. Batin means what is inward, hidden, or spiritual: the deeper meaning. Zahir means what is apparent or outward: the expressed words, the visible form, the literal meaning. The two correspond to the distinct roles of Prophet and Imam.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00478

Twelver Shiism has sought to keep them in perfect balance. The Prophet and the Imam are two lamps lit from the same Light (we will return to this in Chapter VI). The inner meaning cannot exist for us without the outward form that carries it. What a symbol means can reveal itself only through the symbol itself. This was also the position of Ismaili teachers in the Fatimid period.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00479

On this subject, we possess a long letter from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq to his disciple Mufaddal al-Ju'fi, who was disturbed by the extreme views of certain fellow believers. The Imam did not condemn their search for hidden knowledge. He condemned one particular, fundamental mistake. Knowing the inner meaning of prayer, pilgrimage, fasting, and other religious practices does not give us permission to stop practising them. Spiritual knowledge allows the deeper truth (haqiqat) to shine through the rites prescribed by the sacred law (sharia). It makes the very words of the law transparent to their inner meaning.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00480
But that can happen only while both the outward practice and its inward truth remain together.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00481

Break that connection, and spiritual freedom turns into a rejection of all discipline. The living world of symbols is destroyed; in one sense, Adam's mistake is repeated. This is why Imam Ja'far so strongly insisted on preserving the balance between zahir and batin, and why Twelver Shiism would continue to regard that balance as essential.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00482

Yet human history has constantly threatened this balance, precisely because it runs against the grain of ordinary worldly affairs. This conflict is what I mean by the spiritual struggle of Shiism. We have seen that Shiism's deepest secret lies in walayat: the special bond of divine love and devotion that gives the Twelve Imams their spiritual responsibility to preserve and pass on the inner meaning of revelation. Walayat is therefore described as the “inner meaning of the prophetic mission” (batin al-nubuwwat).
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00483

But this leads to an unsettling question. Could the greatest danger facing a religion devoted to hidden spiritual truth be the very thing that seems to promise its success—a victory in the world of politics? Its ultimate triumph belongs, by its nature, to the end of time. If a religion whose hope points beyond ordinary history must adapt itself to the demands of government and public life, will political success bring about a deep crisis in its spiritual teaching?
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00484

Ismailism and Twelver Shiism each faced this paradox, though under very different conditions. For Ismailism, the test came through the success of the Fatimid dynasty in Egypt, between the tenth and twelfth centuries. For Twelver Shiism, it began at the opening of the sixteenth century, when the young Shah Ismail founded the Safavid dynasty, restored Iran's national unity, and established Twelver Shiism as the state religion.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00485

How did Ismailism respond to this trial? This is not the place to examine the gap between the lofty spiritual philosophy found in Ismaili books and the practical necessities of Fatimid rule in Cairo. It is fair to say, without oversimplifying matters, that Fatimid political policy did not in itself favour placing the inner meaning of religion at the centre of attention.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00486

After the death of the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir bi'llah in 487 AH (1094 CE), a bitter crisis split the Ismaili community into two branches. The so-called western branch continued the earlier Fatimid tradition. The eastern branch emerged from the reform proclaimed at Alamut, the famous Ismaili stronghold in the mountains southwest of the Caspian Sea. This was, more particularly, Iranian Ismailism.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00487

What distinguished this reformed Iranian tradition was its willingness to tip the balance decisively towards haqiqat, the inner spiritual truth, and away from sharia, the law governing outward religious practice. It therefore also gave the Imam precedence over the Prophet. This was the meaning of the proclamation of the “Great Resurrection” (Qiyamat al-Qiyamat) at Alamut on 8 August 1164. Recently, a few devoted individuals have been able to mark its eight-hundredth anniversary, making up for the neglect of an age so absorbed in official, outward history that it scarcely notices the events of spiritual history, which escape its control and its usual categories.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00488
Put very simply, the solemn proclamation at Alamut of the personal religion of the Resurrection (Din-e Qiyamat) announced the end of the rule of sharia.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00489

The spirit of the Alamut reform thus stands in sharp contrast to the political Ismailism of the Fatimids. It was, in a sense, a reaction against it. If we compare the surviving documents with the earliest Ismaili writings, we cannot help feeling that the reform recovered something of the spirit of an original, uncompromising Shiism—an understanding of the Imam that existed before the Fatimid dynasty.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00490

Another sign of this spirit appeared after the Mongols destroyed the Alamut organisation and its fortified centres in Iran. Iranian Ismailism went underground and became closely blended with Sufism. Even today, it is regarded, to some extent, as a Sufi tariqa, or spiritual brotherhood. Here, devotion to the Imam unfolds into an experience of mystical love, with the Imam as its centre. Twelver Shiism knows this experience too, for its spiritual life draws upon the same sources.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00491

Consider, for example, the way the Qur'an's Verse of Light (24:35) is interpreted. It speaks of an olive tree that is “neither of the East nor of the West.” In mystical interpretation, this becomes a tree growing at the summit of an inward Mount Sinai. The mountain is the spiritual person, who relives the experience of Moses. And the olive tree represents the Imam: the Soul of the soul, the soul's eternal Beloved.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00492

As this suggests, the flourishing of mystical love is not what separates Ismaili spirituality from that of Twelver Shiism. On both sides, walayat could lead to the same flowering. What gives Twelver spirituality its particular character is the paradox it had to face in order to remain true to itself. More precisely, we shall find that it confronted two related paradoxes.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00493

First, Twelver Shiism has a different understanding of the Imam and of the Imam's relation to the present world. As we have already observed, its complete spiritual company of Imams is fixed at twelve from before the beginning of time. The idea of the Hidden Imam is therefore built into the very meaning of the Imam in Twelver belief.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00494

The Twelfth Imam's spiritual rule stretches across the interval between his past presence and his future return. He is invisibly present within the time of this world, from the moment he disappeared from human sight in 260 AH (874 CE) until the day he appears again. His rule continues on a spiritual plane beyond the reach of the senses, and its daily effects unfold in the hidden depths of human awareness. His position is not comparable to that of the Fatimid Imams, descendants of Imam Ismail, who held political power in Cairo for two centuries—from the rise of Ubaydallah al-Mahdi in 909 to the death of al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah in 1130.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00495

For the same reason, Shah Ismail (1487–1524), the founder of the Safavid dynasty, cannot be compared with the Fatimid Imams. Acting with all the fervour of youth, Shah Ismail acted in the name of the invisible Imam. He restored the Shiite community's right to live openly—its right to bear witness to its faith in this world.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00496
But he was not himself the Imam. The same distinction has applied ever since to every Iranian ruler who has governed a Shiite state.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00497

The ruler's task is to secure for believers the time of their waiting, until the Imam appears again. Becoming a state religion inevitably changed Shiite life from what it had been during the years of secrecy.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00498

Yet the belief that the Imam is essentially invisible makes spiritual life more demanding in a way that differs profoundly from a tradition in which the Imam can be encountered, generation after generation, as a living person in the physical world. By treating the ghaybat—the Imam's concealment or invisibility—as essential to his role, Twelver Shiism places the Imam's reality on an exceptionally high spiritual horizon.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00499

We must go further, because some Western writers have introduced a serious misunderstanding by speaking of “Shiite legitimism,” as though the Imams were simply the rightful claimants in a dynastic struggle. Their cause is not a claim by one earthly dynasty against another. As we have already said, the dynasty of the Grail is no more a rival of an earthly dynasty or of the succession to the Apostolic See. Reducing the matter to competing claims for power misses the point entirely.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00500

Rivalry is possible only between things that exist on the same level. Here we are dealing with two different worlds. The malakut, the spiritual kingdom, stands too far above the world of our political struggles to compete with it.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00501

We can learn something important about this from Qazi Sa'id Qummi (d. 1103 AH/1691 CE), an outstanding scholar of divine wisdom in the Safavid period. In his enormous commentary on a work by Shaykh Saduq Ibn Babuyeh, one of the earliest Shiite teachers, he writes:
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00502

The tradition firmly establishes that God's Messenger was given a choice between being a servant and being a king. He chose to be a prophet who was a servant (abd nabi), not a prophet who was a king (malik nabi). There can therefore be no outward, worldly kingship (saltanat zahira) inherited from him, no rule of the kind exercised by the powerful of this world (imarat al-jababira). If he himself possessed no such kingship, how could anyone who succeeded him inherit it?
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00503

So, if the Prophet has a successor, that succession must necessarily be religious (khilafat diniya). Its purpose is to help believers prepare as well as possible for the journey and the Return. This spiritual kingship (saltanat ma'nawiya) belongs to one who is constant in devotion, one who can truly be called the very soul of the Prophet—as the Prophet himself said of Ali, Hasan, and Husayn.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00504

Nothing could be clearer. This statement expresses, in a particularly direct way, the religious understanding of spiritual Islam held by the Shiite scholars to whom we must turn if we want to understand their tradition.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00505

The Imam's role as a spiritual king, and his essential invisibility in the present condition of the world, both follow from the idea of walayat. That idea will keep returning throughout this work. We must now bring out another part of its meaning, which will prepare us to understand the first of our two paradoxes.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00506

In Shiite writings, the word mahabbat, meaning “love,” often appears alongside walayat, or even takes its place. It describes the devoted love that believers feel for the holy Imams. More precisely, accepting the Imams' walayat is inseparable from recognising the Prophet's mission (nubuwwat), just as recognising that mission is inseparable from affirming God's oneness (tawhid). The profession of faith (shahadat) is therefore, in its fullest form, a threefold declaration. Without all three parts, someone may be a Muslim (muslim), in the sense of professing Islam, but is not yet a true believer (mu'min) in the Shiite sense.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00507

In the devotion shown to the “Holy Family,” then, Shiite Islam reveals itself as a religion of love. This is strikingly different from the mainly legal character often associated with Islam, and which does, to a degree, correspond to the general approach of Sunni Islam.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00508

But Shiite teachers rely on their most explicit traditions to make an even stronger claim: without the loving intention and devoted service contained in walayat, no good deed can receive God's acceptance.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00509

In this respect, Shiism—which has so often been presented as the opposite of Sufism—was already following the path of love before Sufism came to be identified with it. Yet this immediately raises a serious question. If many deeply devoted Shiites have indeed expressed misgivings about Sufism, what was the relationship between Shiism and Sufism at their beginnings?
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00510

One of the hardest questions Sufism had to face was whether love—the word itself, as well as the feeling—could properly describe the relationship between a human being and God. We will encounter this question again in Book III, when we study Ruzbihan. The answers given by different thinkers varied widely.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00511

Here, however, we must make an essential point. Shiism insists, through its understanding of what cannot be said about God, that God's oneness (tawhid) places the divine reality absolutely beyond our grasp.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00512

But it is precisely the teaching about the Imams that keeps this belief from falling into two opposite traps. One is to say that God is so unknowable that nothing meaningful can be known or said about the divine. The other is to imagine God too easily in human terms. Both, in different ways, distort our understanding of God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00513

Shiism avoids these traps by recognising the pre-eternal spiritual reality of the Imams as the place where God's Names and Attributes become manifest. In the Imam, the believer contemplates the revealed “Face” of God. We introduced this idea of the divine Face in Chapter I, Section 3, and will return to it. From its beginnings, then, and before Sufism had even worked through the problem, Shiism had found a way to understand the love that can exist between a human creature and a God who, in himself, remains beyond all reach.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00514

All this is contained in walayat, understood as the inner meaning of the prophetic message, and in the Imam's role as the guide who leads us into the inner world (batin). But by “inner world” I do not mean something merely private or subjective, as opposed to something objective and real.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00515

That may be difficult to explain today. There is a kind of disbelief that still calls itself Christian yet speaks contemptuously of “inward and subjective religiosity.” Its advocates are so absorbed in their “engagement” with the affairs of this world that they have never taken the time to understand what they dismiss. For the spiritual thinkers we are studying, the inner world means the spiritual reality of worlds beyond the senses. Far from being less real than the outer world, this spiritual reality surrounds and contains it.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00516

Qazi Sa'id Qummi gives this surprising idea particular emphasis. In the circles of the spiritual worlds, unlike those of the material world, the centre surrounds the circumference. To “leave” what we normally call the outer world is not merely a subjective experience. It is, in the fullest possible sense, an experience of reality—however difficult that may be to convey to someone determined to think of themselves as “modern.”
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00517

Even so, Shiism has not always been free, throughout its history, to express openly the essential character I have just sketched. We said earlier that it too had to face a trial and a paradox resembling those faced by Ismailism under the Fatimids.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00518

Yet the trial was bound to take a different form. We have already seen why, and we shall return to the matter: the Twelver understanding of the Imam and his spiritual authority is shaped above all by the Twelfth Imam and the belief that his concealment (ghaybat) is necessary.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00519

For a long time, Shiites were forced to practise their faith in varying degrees of secrecy. With the restoration of Iranian sovereignty under the Safavids, however, they could at last live openly. Such a change brings a powerful temptation to settle comfortably into this world. And the more comfortable our place in this world becomes, the less likely we are to give our full attention to the questions that matter most to thinkers concerned with spiritual wisdom.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00520

Perhaps this helps explain the paradoxical growth, within Shiism, of fiqh, the study of religious law, at the expense of irfan and hikmat ilahiya: inner spiritual knowledge and divine wisdom, both taught by the Imams themselves. Yet the tradition of the hukama and the urafa—the sages and those devoted to inner knowledge—has never been broken, right down to our own day. It remains something distinctive in Islam. We will return to this vital part of Shiism's spiritual struggle.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00521

At first sight, then, the situation might seem quite simple. On one side stand those devoted to the spiritual life, who remain faithful to what they see as the whole of Shiism: both its outward practice and its inner meaning. Broadly speaking, these are the urafa and hukama, the mystics and the philosophers of divine wisdom. In Book II, we shall see how Suhrawardi distinguished different levels among them.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00522

On the other side stand those who, for one reason or another, distrust anything they regard as “philosophy.” They devote themselves to fiqh, religious law, almost as though it were the only truly Islamic field of knowledge. These are the fuqaha, the scholars of the Law. Their fellow Shiites have more than once accused them of a profound inconsistency: they claim to teach the Imams' religion while setting aside an essential part of the Imams' own teaching.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00523

But the real situation is more complicated than this division suggests. Much of the difficulty arises from the uncertain relationship between Shiism and Sufism at their beginnings, one cause of which we have already touched upon.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00524

In Sunni Islam, the broad pattern is easier to recognise. Over the centuries, Sufism and the Sufis have stood, in contrast to the scholars of religious law, for the daring possibilities of inner religion and the seeming contradictions of a faith rooted in love. In Shiite Islam, matters are not so simple. From the very beginning, walayat has stood at the heart of Shiite teaching. As a result, that teaching already includes everything needed for a religion of love directed towards a divine manifestation: the revealed Face of God, who in himself is beyond all knowledge, the Person who can “answer on behalf of” the unreachable God.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00525

As a point of orientation, this same Face guides the mystic on an ascent through the spiritual worlds that it reveals. As the spiritual centre, the invisible Imam gathers around himself an entire order of spiritual beings who, like him, remain hidden from the eyes of this world. All these ideas can also be found in Sufism and its spiritual philosophy. Indeed, Sunni Sufism can sometimes give the impression of being a kind of Shiism that no longer dares to call itself Shiite.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00526

And yet this is precisely why someone who lives the fullness of Shiite faith has no need to become a Sufi as such. Shiism already offers a tariqa, a spiritual path, as we suggested in Chapter I, Section 3 (pp. 18 onward). In other words, Sufism (tasawwuf) does not embrace the whole of mystical life in Islam. That brings us back to the question raised earlier: what, at their beginnings, was the relationship between Shiism and Sufism? Or, to put it another way, what were the beginnings of spiritual Islam?
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00527

Simply asking the question clearly helps us avoid confusion. The existence of Shiite Sufism does not, by itself, answer it. Nor should we assume that a Shiite theologian who has reservations about Sufism—even strong ones—must belong to the legal scholars who oppose mysticism. Far from it. Many Shiite spiritual thinkers speak the same language as the Sufis without being Sufis themselves. They belong to no Sufi tariqa.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00528

Mulla Sadra Shirazi, one of the greatest Iranian thinkers of divine wisdom, even found it necessary to write a book against the Sufis of his own day. At the same time, some of his colleagues accused him of being a Sufi. Sufism itself takes many forms. Some Sufi traditions have developed an extraordinary understanding of spiritual reality, tested and confirmed through lived experience. Others dismiss this kind of philosophical understanding altogether. In some, devotion to the Imams is central. In others, the figure of the Sufi master (shaykh) tends to take the place of the Imams' transcendent spiritual presence.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00529

We can therefore speak of a double paradox. First, there is the paradox of religious-law scholars who have lost sight of the full meaning of Shiism and its inner spiritual foundation. This problem grew worse after the Safavid period, though its signs were visible earlier, just as the great schools of thought of the Safavid age had themselves been prepared by previous generations. Second, there is the paradox of forms of Sufism that have forgotten their own origins.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00530

Caught between these two, many Shiite spiritual thinkers had to struggle on two fronts at once. This was true of Mulla Sadra Shirazi and many others, right through to the Shaykhi school. Earlier still, it was especially true of Haydar Amoli, who lived in the eighth/fourteenth century. In his great body of work, he brought together the problems faced by Shiite spiritual thinkers and understood them with remarkable clarity (see Book IV). That is why we shall turn to his writings so often in the pages ahead.
